title: The Convenient Argument
author: Caiti Wade
summary: Caiti Wade of The Disruptive Educator uses a rereading of Jane Austen as a frame for showing how critics of explicit instruction win arguments nobody was making. She names four literary devices that appear in education discourse: caricature, loaded language, false dichotomy and semantic substitution. The caricature turns an advocate of explicit instruction into a rigid, scripted, joyless figure, and she distinguishes capital-D Direct Instruction, which uses scripts, from explicit teaching, which need not. Loaded words such as mandate, dogma and zealot, and clickbait headlines, let a writer persuade without demonstrating that a practice is harmful. False dichotomies set knowledge against creativity or academics against wellbeing, and semantic substitution swaps a practice for the value it serves so that questioning the practice sounds like opposing the value. She concludes that explicit instruction and the science of learning should be open to criticism, but only if opponents represent positions accurately and separate practices from values.
points: Critics often construct a caricature of the explicit instruction advocate as rigid, scripted and indifferent to children, which makes the position far easier to dismiss than the real one.
Capital-D Direct Instruction involves a script, but explicit and direct instruction does not have to, and structured lessons need not rob teachers of artistry any more than a score robs a musician.
Loaded language and provocative headlines can do the arguing for a writer, so readers should check the underlying report before reacting to the framing.
False dichotomies such as academics versus wellbeing recast a debate about instructional effectiveness as a debate about whether you care about children.
Semantic substitution turns a question about a practice, such as restorative conversations versus consequences, into an accusation that the questioner opposes the value itself.
quotes: Dear reader, if you’ve found yourself defending your commitment to a value when all you did was question a practice, I’m afraid someone has rather quietly changed the subject.
Incorrect. Direct Instruction (capital D; capital I) involves using a script. “Explicit and direct instruction” does not have to.

Of course, these caricatures aren’t real. Sure, it’s quite likely desks are in rows for most learning, and there’s a good chance there’s some rote memorisation included, but would you believe you can do all of those things and still run a lesson that’s responsive to students in the room and even fun?
But there’s a rather important difference between using provocative language to draw attention to an argument and using it to do the arguing for you.
Believe it or not, you can care about academics and still prioritise wellbeing. In fact, I’d go as far as to say I focus on teaching academics well as part of my prioritisation of student wellbeing.

This shifts the debate. It’s not about the relative merits of different instructional approaches anymore. Now the conversation is about whether you care about students, value their individuality, respect their autonomy or believe they deserve exposure to “real world” problems.

Rather than defending the evidence for a practice, the writer gets to defend a value nobody was disputing in the first place. And the person asking perfectly reasonable questions about effectiveness is left explaining that they do, in fact, care about children.

However, to actually have those discussions, they require us to represent opposing positions accurately, distinguish practices from values, and engage with what people actually believe, rather than what we would prefer them to believe.
